If you imagine a resident of the borough trying to live in the woods you get an idea of the challenge. Living in the woods isn't *hard*, but if you didn't think to chop firewood or fix the insulation or stock up on some staples and preserves because you thought that (respectively) the landlord would just turn the heat on and the super would fix the insulation and you could get away with ordering Chinese delivery or groceries during a two-day blizzard...then you are going to think that country living means freezing and starving. 

Likewise, newcomers don't anticipate the huge learning curve. They don't know not to rent an apartment above a restaurant (noise and vermin). They don't know not to enter the empty subway car at rush hour (smelly homeless guy). They don't know where to go when you are out and have to pee. The don't know where to affordably shop when they're used to big-box stores and now they're in a city where you get your meat, cheese, wine, produce, hardware, etc all at different small shops. They don't know that the trains change routes on the weekends and late nights and end up stranded in a remote neighborhood waiting for a return trip. They don't know that a tourist delaying you for thirty seconds can magically make you thirty minutes late for work. They don't know that owning a car means getting up at 7 every morning to move it and that it's probably not worth keeping. They don't know how to interact with the super, or what they are legally entitled to as tenants. They don't know that there are a bunch of local festivals and parades that shut down certain parts of the city at the same time every year, so they end up late for work on the day of the parade and have no idea why. 

They do a whole bunch of absent-minded things, go unnecessarily out of their way, and work way harder than they have to, because they don't know any better. 

Those are all things that to a local are no big deal and are easily dealt with/avoided, the same way a person in a suburb knows to grab dinner before 8 pm because all the places close at 9. You stay here long enough and the inconveniences are all instinctually avoided. Quality of life improves DRAMATICALLY for people who stick it out and learn the ropes. For people who already have decent street smarts adjusting can be very quick, but most people coming from suburbs typically have very little sense of space or situational awareness to begin with so the city just overwhelms them. 

Transplants also don't know how to take advantage of all the amazing stuff here. Just as an example, entertainment: They pay full-price (or use a discount service for meager discounts) to see the biggest hit Broadway shows, then bemoan only seeing one show a year because of how expensive it is ($79-500 a ticket) - meanwhile locals use papering services for free tickets or stay informed on new shows or better lesser-known shows, or else they've made connected friends. I've been going on twice-weekly dates to see big band concerts, ballets, major sporting events, cruises, Broadway shows, and gallery openings, and in four months I've never spent more than ten dollars to get in. Not ten dollars a person - ten dollars. For the whole date. There are also all sorts of amazingly cheap and free things to do - during the summer there are around 15 different free shows, concerts, screenings, gallery openings, or other events to go to *every night*. Several of the museums that people shell out $35 dollars for are technically pay-what-you-want. Operas often have $20 tickets. If you do the city right it's one of the cheapest places in the country to go on a really swanky date. I can't think of anywhere else in the country where a person poor enough to go on Medicaid could justify regularly attending swanky concerts by world-class musicians in their budget, but you can do that here. Shit, I pay less to take a date out to the opera or to a great concert or a gallery opening (with FREE WINE) than most people spend to take their date to a movie theater. 

Locals also start to realize when it's a good idea to get out of town, or where in the city they can get away from it all. Or what parts of town are all tourists.
